solution:
Electron gain enthalpy is negative for the halogens, and "highest" here means the most negative (the largest energy release on adding an electron). Table 7.3 of the chapter lists \(\Delta_{eg}H\) in kJ/mol as F \(-333\), Cl \(-349\), Br \(-325\), I \(-296\). Chlorine at \(-349\) is the most negative, so **B** is correct.

The other three fail on the same table: iodine \((-296)\) is the least negative of the four, bromine \((-325)\) is less negative than chlorine, and fluorine \((-333)\) — the option the periodic trend tempts you into — is also less negative than chlorine. The chapter states the reason outright: "In group 17, fluorine has less negative electron gain enthalpy than that of chlorine. This is due to small size of fluorine atom", the incoming electron meeting strong inter-electronic repulsion in the compact 2p shell.

The chapter states that for the group 16 hydrides "the acidic character of the hydrides increases, while thermal stability decreases from \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\)", because the H–E bond dissociation enthalpy falls down the group (Table 7.5: 463, 347, 276, 238 kJ/mol). A weaker H–E bond releases \(\mathrm{H^+}\) more readily, so acidity runs \(\mathrm{H_2Te > H_2Se > H_2S > H_2O}\) — which is **C**. The same table's \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) row confirms it numerically: 14.0, 7.0, 3.8, 2.6, i.e. \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\) is the strongest acid and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) the weakest.

A is the exact reverse of the measured order. B and D each place \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) above \(\mathrm{H_2S}\) or \(\mathrm{H_2Se}\), contradicting \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 14.0 for water against 7.0 and 3.8 for the others.

Section 7.6.1 of the chapter says that oxygen "shows \(-2\), \(-1\), and \(+2\) oxidation states while other elements show \(-2\), \(+2\), \(+4\), \(+6\) oxidation states", and gives the reason: "Oxygen can not exhibit higher oxidation state due to absence of vacant d orbitals." So oxygen is the one group 16 element that never reaches \(+4\), and **A** is correct.

S, Se and Te (options B, C, D) all have vacant d orbitals in their valence shells and are named by the chapter as showing \(+4\) and \(+6\); the chapter also lists concrete \(+4\) compounds for each — \(\mathrm{SO_2}\), \(\mathrm{SeO_2}\), \(\mathrm{TeO_2}\), and the tetrahalides \(\mathrm{SF_4}\), \(\mathrm{SeF_4}\), \(\mathrm{TeF_4}\).

Concentrated sulfuric acid is an oxidising agent, and the chapter's own worked example (Problem 7.10) gives the reaction: \(2\mathrm{HI} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{I_2} + \mathrm{SO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\). The iodide is oxidised to free iodine while the sulfur is reduced from \(+6\) to \(+4\). Hence **C**.

A (\(\mathrm{HIO_3}\)) would require iodine to be oxidised all the way to \(+5\), which the chapter attributes to chlorine water \((\mathrm{I_2} + 6\mathrm{H_2O} + 5\mathrm{Cl_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{HIO_3} + 10\mathrm{HCl})\), not to sulfuric acid. B and D both name a potassium salt, and no potassium is present anywhere in the reactants.

The chapter gives one balanced ozone-destroying reaction, twice: \(\mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{O_3(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}\), adding that "the nitrogen oxide emitted from the exhaust systems of supersonic jet aeroplanes can bringforth depletion of ozone layer in the upper atmosphere". Nitric oxide, NO, is therefore the depleting species and **A** is correct.

\(\mathrm{NO_2}\) (B) appears in the chapter only as the *product* of that reaction, not the attacking species; \(\mathrm{NO_3}\) (C) and \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) (D) are named nowhere in the chapter's account of ozone depletion, whose only other stated cause is chlorofluorocarbons.

Among the anomalous properties of fluorine the chapter states: "Hydrogen fluoride is a liquid (b.p. 293 K) due to strong hydrogen bonding while other hydrogen halides are gases." HF is the only hydrogen halide held together by hydrogen bonding, so it alone is a liquid at ordinary room temperature. Hence **D**.

Table 7.6 rules out B and C directly — HCl boils at 189 K and HBr at 206 K, far below room temperature, so both are gases. A, \(\mathrm{HIO_3}\) (iodic acid), is not a hydrogen halide at all; the chapter lists it among the oxoacids isolated "in pure form", i.e. as a solid.

[Textbook misprint: the question asks about "pyrosulfurous acid". The chapter names no such acid; the only "pyro" acid of sulfur it teaches is "Di or pyrosulfuric acid, \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}\)" (section 7.8.1), for which the answer is \(+6\). Read literally as pyrosulfurous acid, \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_5}\), the question would have no correct option at all.]

The only "pyro" acid of sulfur this chapter teaches is item (iii) of section 7.8.1, "Di or pyrosulfuric acid, \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}\)". Taking H as \(+1\) and O as \(-2\): \(2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0\), so \(2x = 12\) and \(x = +6\) for **both** sulfur atoms. The oxidation state is therefore \(+6\) only, which is **D**.

The other three fail on that arithmetic: \(+2\) (A) and \(+4\) (B) are each too low to balance the seven oxygens, and C requires the two sulfur atoms to differ, whereas in \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}\) they are equivalent — each is a \(\mathrm{-SO_3H}\) unit joined through a bridging oxygen, as the chapter's printed structure shows.

[Textbook misprint: option B is printed as "IBr > BeF > ICl > ClF > BrCl". "BeF" should read "BrF" — beryllium fluoride is not a halogen compound and cannot appear in an ordering of interhalogens. The option is a distractor either way; the correct order is the one in option C.]

The chapter's table of properties of interhalogen compounds gives the thermal-stability row verbatim as \(\mathrm{ClF > ICl > IBr > BrCl > BrF}\). That is option **C**, character for character.

A is close to the reverse of it, putting the least stable member BrF first. D moves ICl ahead of ClF and BrCl ahead of IBr, neither of which matches the printed order. B is not a valid ordering of interhalogens at all — see the bracketed note on the question, where "BeF" is a misprint. The trend itself is sensible: stability tracks the electronegativity difference between the two halogens, largest for Cl–F and smallest for Br–F, whose two atoms are of similar size and bond weakly.

Hydrolysis of an interhalogen compound gives the oxoacid of the **larger, more electropositive** halogen and the halogen acid of the smaller one. The chapter prints this exact case: \(\mathrm{BrCl} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HOBr} + \mathrm{HCl}\). Bromine, being the more electropositive of the pair, ends up in HOBr and chlorine in HCl, so both products form together and **D** is correct.

C gives only half the equation and leaves the chlorine unaccounted for. A puts bromine in the halogen acid, inverting the roles the chapter's rule assigns. B describes a redox split into the free halogens, which is not what hydrolysis does — no water would be consumed.

The chapter's table of methods of preparation lists, under direct combination, \(\mathrm{Cl_2} + 3\mathrm{F_2}\ (\text{excess}) \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{ClF_3}\). With fluorine in excess chlorine takes its higher oxidation state \(+3\), giving \(\mathrm{ClF_3}\). Hence **B**.

A, ClF, is what forms when the two gases are used in *equal volumes* — the same table gives \(\mathrm{Cl_2} + \mathrm{F_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{ClF}\) — so it is the wrong stoichiometry for excess fluorine. C and D are not interhalogen compounds at all: the chapter states that an interhalogen has an even total number of atoms and an odd number of \(\mathrm{X'}\) atoms, which rules out both \(\mathrm{ClF_2}\) (3 atoms, 2 fluorines) and \(\mathrm{Cl_2F_3}\) (5 atoms, two central halogens).

In the general formula \(\mathrm{XX'_n}\) the chapter defines X as "the halogen having larger size and is more electropositive" and \(\mathrm{X'}\) as "the halogen having smaller size and more electronegativity"; X is the central atom. Fluorine is both the smallest halogen (atomic radius 64 pm, Table 7.3) and the most electronegative element in the periodic table, so it can only ever be \(\mathrm{X'}\), never the centre. Hence **D**.

Table 7.9 confirms it by exhaustion: every compound listed there — ClF, \(\mathrm{ClF_3}\), \(\mathrm{ClF_5}\), BrF, \(\mathrm{BrF_3}\), \(\mathrm{BrF_5}\), BrCl, IF, \(\mathrm{IF_3}\), \(\mathrm{IF_5}\), \(\mathrm{IF_7}\), ICl, \(\mathrm{ICl_3}\), IBr — has fluorine only as the terminal atom, while Cl (A is I, B is Cl, C is Br), Br and I each appear as a central atom in that same table.

Table 7.12 of the chapter tabulates the number of lone pairs on the central halogen against its oxidation state: \(+7\) has 0, \(+5\) has 1, \(+3\) has 2 and \(+1\) has 3. One lone pair therefore means an \(\mathrm{XX'_5}\) compound, and the table names \(\mathrm{ClF_5}\), \(\mathrm{BrF_5}\) and \(\mathrm{IF_5}\) as its examples. Of the four options only \(\mathrm{IF_5}\) is of that type, so **C**.

Counting from the same table: A, \(\mathrm{IF_3}\), has iodine at \(+3\) and so carries 2 lone pairs; D, \(\mathrm{ClF_3}\), likewise 2; B, ICl, has iodine at \(+1\) and carries 3. Only C has exactly one.

[Textbook misprint: options A and D are printed as \(\mathrm{[I_3]}\) and \(\mathrm{[BrF_4]}\), without their charges. Both species are ANIONS — \(\mathrm{[I_3]^-}\) and \(\mathrm{[BrF_4]^-}\) — and the electron count that fixes their shapes depends on that charge.]

Take the options one at a time. B and C are refuted directly by Table 7.11, which prints \(\mathrm{BrF_5}\) as **square pyramidal** (not trigonal bipyramidal) and \(\mathrm{ClF_3}\) as **bent T-shaped** (not trigonal planar). A is wrong because the triiodide ion has 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs on the central iodine; the three lone pairs occupy the equatorial positions of a trigonal bipyramid and the two bonds go axial, giving a **linear** ion, not a bent one. That leaves **D**.

D is right on its own merits, not merely by elimination: in \(\mathrm{[BrF_4]^-}\) the central bromine has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs. The two lone pairs take opposite axial positions of an octahedron and the four fluorines lie in the remaining plane, giving a square planar ion — exactly the arrangement the chapter draws for the isoelectronic \(\mathrm{XeF_4}\) in Table 7.13, which it also labels square planar.

The chapter states as a general characteristic that "interhalogen compounds have even number of atoms 2, 4, 6, 8", and its classification lists four types — \(\mathrm{XX'}\), \(\mathrm{XX'_3}\), \(\mathrm{XX'_5}\) and \(\mathrm{XX'_7}\) — of which the largest, \(\mathrm{XX'_7}\), is represented by the single compound \(\mathrm{IF_7}\). One iodine plus seven fluorines is 8 atoms, so **D**.

A (3) and C (7) are both odd and so are excluded by the even-atom rule before any counting; B (6) is the size of an \(\mathrm{XX'_5}\) compound such as \(\mathrm{IF_5}\), which the chapter lists but which is not the largest type.
